projects.title: Sybil-Resilient Model Extraction Detection
projects.label: master's capstone · ML security
projects.one_line: Catching model-stealing attacks that hide across many fake (Sybil) accounts.
projects.headline_text: Sybil accounts caught: PRADA alone vs with my detection layer
projects.ask_keywords: capstone, sybil, model extraction, model stealing, prada, ml security
projects.intro: An extension of PRADA (Juuti et al., EuroS&P 2019), tested on an MNIST classifier. My master's capstone at Rutgers.
projects.question: PRADA spots model-stealing by checking whether an account's query distances look normally distributed. An attacker can split queries across fake (Sybil) accounts so each one stays under PRADA's 100-query warm-up and never gets checked.
projects.what_i_did: A second detection layer that compares query-distance histograms across accounts using Jensen-Shannon divergence. Sybil accounts all send Jacobian-generated images, so their histograms converge. Benign accounts' histograms don't.
projects.result: PRADA alone flagged **0 of 64** Sybil accounts. With the JS layer, detection held from 4 to 128 accounts with zero false positives.

key_numbers.label: Sybil accounts caught by PRADA alone
label agreement between the attacker's copy and the victim model

projects.recommendation: Run a cross-account check like this alongside per-account detection on any public model API, and re-tune the threshold on held-out traffic before relying on it in production.

images.alt: Detection rate vs number of Sybil accounts
images.caption: Detection rate as the attack is split across more fake accounts. PRADA alone drops to 0% at 64 accounts. The JS layer keeps firing, but from about 192 accounts up its separation signal weakens (see limitations below).

images.alt: PRADA W scores, attackers vs benign
images.caption: PRADA's single-account baseline. Attacker accounts score below the 0.96 threshold and get flagged. The benign account (0.9864) stays clean.

extra_sections.heading: How the test bed works
extra_sections.html: A CNN victim model (99.08% MNIST test accuracy) is served through a FastAPI endpoint that logs every query. A Papernot Jacobian-based attack runs 6 augmentation rounds to train a substitute model. PRADA (distance computation plus a Shapiro-Wilk test) and the JS layer are evaluated side by side, including a benign-user baseline and three query distributions: round-robin, randomized, and mixed 70/30.

extra_sections.heading: What it can't do
extra_sections.html:
• At 192 or more Sybil accounts, per-account histograms get sparse and the JS separation gap collapses, so detection becomes unstable.
  • A mixed 70/30 attack shrinks the separation gap to 0.002 in some configurations. Still detected, but the margin is thin.
  • The JS threshold (0.15) was tuned on the same data used for evaluation. There is no held-out test set.
  • PRADA's AUC of 1.0 comes from only two W scores, so I don't treat it as a robust result.

projects.title: Olist Delivery Performance

projects.one_line: Where are deliveries late, and do customers notice?
projects.headline_text: correlation between late delivery and review score
projects.ask_keywords: olist, delivery, late delivery, e commerce, ecommerce, brazil, review score
projects.intro: 99,441 Brazilian e-commerce orders across Brazil's 26 states and the Federal District, and 70+ product categories.
projects.question: Which product categories and regions have the highest late-delivery rates, and does that line up with lower review scores? Written for two audiences: Logistics and Customer Experience.
projects.what_i_did: Joined the orders, customers, order items, products and reviews tables in PostgreSQL. projects.result: Alagoas had the worst late rate at **23.0%** of orders. Electronics led categories at 9.6%. Late delivery and review score showed a moderate negative correlation of -0.327.

late rate for electronics, the worst category
correlation, late delivery vs review score

projects.recommendation: Start with Alagoas and the electronics category, where late rates are highest. Since late orders track with lower review scores, add seller-level data next, and carrier data if it can be sourced, to find out why those orders run late.

images.alt: Olist delivery performance dashboard in Power BI
images.caption: My Power BI dashboard: late rate by state and by category, late rate vs average review score, and the worst category in the five high-volume states.

extra_sections.heading: Limits
extra_sections.html: This locates where delivery problems are worst. It doesn't claim a root cause: seller-level performance wasn't part of this analysis, and warehouse and carrier data aren't in the dataset. The worst-category-per-state ranking is only reliable for the five high-volume states: MG, PR, RJ, RS and SP.

projects.title: F1 Pit Stop Strategy
projects.label: SQL + DAX
projects.one_line: Do faster pit stops actually win races?
projects.headline_text: correlation between total pit lane time and finishing position: more time, slightly worse finish (weak)
projects.ask_keywords: f1, formula 1, formula one, pit stop, racing, motorsport, constructor
projects.intro: 10,884 Formula 1 pit stops from 2011 to 2024, across six PostgreSQL tables.
projects.question: Does pit stop speed relate to where a driver finishes, and have stops gotten faster over the years?
projects.what_i_did: Tested the link at three levels (single stop, race average, race total) with CORR(), compared constructors with AVG and STDDEV, and tracked year-over-year change with LAG. In Power BI I rebuilt the Pearson correlation by hand in DAX and matched SQL's 0.175.
projects.result: The link is weak: **+0.135 to +0.175**. P1 finishers averaged 43.2s of pit lane time per race vs 57.0s for P18, but top teams tend to have both faster cars and faster crews, so pit speed alone doesn't explain results.

key_numbers.label: strongest correlation, total pit lane time vs finish
pit lane time got 1.29s slower from 2013 to 2014, the biggest year-over-year change
Red Bull average pit lane time (entry to exit), fastest and most consistent

projects.recommendation: Don't treat pit-crew speed alone as a lever for race results. Some teams' problem is consistency rather than speed: Aston Martin is mid-pack on speed but second-worst on variability, so that's where they have the most to gain.

images.alt: F1 pit stop strategy dashboard in Power BI
images.caption: My Power BI dashboard: pit lane time by finishing position and by season, plus speed vs consistency by constructor.

extra_sections.heading: Data cleaning
extra_sections.html: Stops of 100 seconds or longer were filtered out as red-flag and safety-car artifacts, so they wouldn't distort the averages.

change in cold teams' road win rate above 75°F (no drop)

projects.recommendation: For warm-weather teams, cold road games are where results drop, so that is where extra preparation pays off. Cold-weather teams don't need to treat heat as a special risk.

projects.label: machine learning
projects.one_line: Predicting house prices, and explaining each prediction in plain terms.
projects.ask_keywords: housing, house price, home price, real estate, ames, explainable
projects.intro: Ames, Iowa housing data: 2,930 homes with about 80 variables each.
projects.question: Can I predict sale prices accurately and still explain, for any one house, why the model priced it that way?
projects.what_i_did: Compared Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM, tuned with GridSearchCV, then used SHAP to explain individual predictions and rank the features that move price most.

projects.recommendation: For a pricing tool, lead with overall quality and living area, and show the SHAP breakdown so an agent can explain each valuation to a buyer or seller.

projects.title: EvoStruct-Sub Protein Localization
projects.label: machine learning · bioinformatics
projects.one_line: Predicting where a protein ends up in or around a bacterial cell, from its sequence.
projects.headline_text: best 10-fold cross-validated accuracy (SVM), across three models
projects.ask_keywords: evostruct, protein, bioinformatics, biology, localization, bacteria
projects.intro: Applies the published EvoStruct-Sub method to a benchmark of 523 Gram-positive bacterial proteins in four subcellular locations. A Rutgers course project.
projects.question: Given only a protein's amino-acid sequence, can a model predict which of four locations it belongs to: cell membrane, cell wall, cytoplasm or extracellular?
projects.what_i_did: Combined evolutionary features from PSI-BLAST (PSSM) with structural features from SPIDER 2.0 into a 235-feature matrix, then trained and compared KNN, SVM and Random Forest with 10-fold cross-validation.
projects.result: Cross-validated accuracy: SVM **70.6%**, Random Forest 69.9%, KNN 66.0%. Accuracy on the training data was much higher (Random Forest 99.23%), which shows overfitting, so I report the cross-validated numbers.
projects.recommendation: Judge models on cross-validated accuracy, not training accuracy. To move past about 70%, tackle the class imbalance first (only 18 cell wall proteins) and reduce overfitting before adding more models.

extra_sections.heading: Reproducibility
extra_sections.html: Pre-extracted features and trained models are in the repo, so the classifiers run in about 10 minutes without the external tools. Rebuilding features from raw sequences needs PSI-BLAST and SPIDER 2.0 and takes several hours.

projects.title: Metaheuristic Algorithm Comparison
projects.label: optimization
projects.one_line: Four nature-inspired optimizers, one classification task: which trains a better model?
projects.headline_text: test accuracy for Wolf Pack and PSO
projects.ask_keywords: metaheuristic, optimizer, optimization algorithm, genetic algorithm, particle swarm, pso, wolf pack, grasshopper
projects.intro: Breast cancer classification on the UCI dataset.
projects.question: Instead of gradient descent, how well do metaheuristic optimizers train a classifier, and which one generalizes best?
projects.what_i_did: Implemented and compared the Grasshopper Optimization Algorithm, Wolf Pack Optimization, Particle Swarm Optimization and a Genetic Algorithm, tracking train and test accuracy and loss for each.
projects.result: In a single run, Wolf Pack and PSO tied at **97.37%** test accuracy, the Genetic Algorithm reached 96.49%, and Grasshopper lagged at 71.05%.
projects.recommendation: Use Wolf Pack or PSO for this kind of problem. Grasshopper needs parameter tuning before it is competitive.

images.caption: Train vs test accuracy and training loss for each optimizer, from the project notebook.
